# The Rector of Justin
## Introduction
*The Rector of Justin* is a psychological fiction novel written by the American attorney and author Louis Auchincloss, first published in 1964 by Houghton Mifflin . Widely considered to be Auchincloss's *magnum opus* and one of the defining texts of mid-20th-century American literature, the novel offers a comprehensive and multifaceted examination of the life of the Reverend Francis "Frank" Prescott, the founder and headmaster of Justin Martyr, an exclusive Episcopal boarding school for boys in Massachusetts . Through a complex narrative structure that utilizes journals, memoirs, letters, and interviews from six distinct narrators, Auchincloss constructs a portrait of a "Great Man" that is as critical as it is admiring, exploring the nuances of charismatic leadership, the burden of legacy, and the twilight of the White Anglo-Saxon Protestant (WASP) aristocracy .

Upon its release, the novel achieved immediate commercial success and critical acclaim. It secured a position on *The New York Times* Best Seller list for thirty-five weeks, eventually reaching the number one spot, and was hailed by *Harper's Magazine* as "almost certainly the finest work ever written about an American preparatory school" . In the literary awards circuit of 1965, *The Rector of Justin* was a finalist for both the National Book Award for Fiction and the Pulitzer Prize for Fiction, competitions that placed it alongside Saul Bellow’s *Herzog* and Shirley Ann Grau’s *The Keepers of the House*.1 The novel's publication marked a pivotal moment in American letters, representing the culmination of the realist "novel of manners" tradition reminiscent of Edith Wharton and Henry James, just as the literary landscape was shifting toward the postmodern and the countercultural .

Set primarily in the cloistered environment of a New England boarding school during the early years of World War II, with extensive flashbacks spanning the late 19th and early 20th centuries, the work serves as both a character study of a formidable educational autocrat and a sociological treatise on the American elite . While Francis Prescott is the gravitational center of the narrative, the novel is equally concerned with the orbit of students, family members, colleagues, and donors whose lives are irrevocably shaped—and occasionally destroyed—by his influence .

## Publication History and Context
### Origins and Authorship
Louis Auchincloss (1917–2010) was uniquely positioned to write *The Rector of Justin*. A member of the "old New York" society he frequently chronicled, Auchincloss was educated at St. Bernard's School, Groton School, and Yale University, followed by law school at the University of Virginia . His dual career as a practicing lawyer at a prestigious Wall Street firm and a prolific novelist allowed him to write with an insider's authority on the mores, hypocrisies, and unspoken codes of the American upper class . By the time *The Rector of Justin* was published, Auchincloss had already written significantly about this milieu, but this novel represented a deepening of his thematic scope, moving from social satire to a more profound investigation of character and moral legacy .

The novel was published on July 10, 1964 . This timing is historically significant, as the cultural dominance of the WASP establishment—the very world Prescott embodies and defends—was beginning to wane in the face of the social upheavals of the 1960s . The book can be read as an elegy for a dying order, a "golden era of once aristocratic New England boarding schools" that was being swept away by egalitarianism and changing social norms .

### Editions
The first edition was released in hardcover by Houghton Mifflin. Its enduring popularity has led to numerous reprintings and special editions over the decades.

| Publisher | Year | Format | Notes | Source |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **Houghton Mifflin** | 1964 | Hardcover | First Edition; Red cloth binding | 1 |
| **Franklin Library** | 1977 | Leather-bound | Signed Limited Edition; Gold embossing | 12 |
| **Mariner Books** | 2002 | Paperback | Modern trade paperback | 2 |
| **Harper Perennial** | 2013 | Paperback | Contemporary reissue | 13 |

The physical presentation of the early editions, particularly the Franklin Library version with its leather binding and gilt edges, underscored the novel's status as a modern classic and an artifact of the very establishment it depicts .

## Narrative Structure
The structural ingenuity of *The Rector of Justin* is central to its thematic execution. Rather than employing a single omniscient narrator or a linear timeline, Auchincloss constructs the novel as a "biography in progress" . The frame narrator is Brian Aspinwall, a young, somewhat timid English teacher who joins the staff of Justin Martyr in 1939 . Aspinwall is tasked—both by his own devotion and by the request of others—to write a biography of the school's eighty-year-old founder, Francis Prescott .

To accomplish this, Aspinwall assembles a "dossier" of documents that provide competing and often contradictory perspectives on the Rector . This polyphonic approach allows Auchincloss to explore the relativity of truth and the complexity of human character. Prescott is seen variously as a saint, a bully, a visionary, a manipulator, a father figure, and a destroyer . The novel is thus not merely a story about a headmaster, but a meta-narrative about the impossibility of fully knowing another human being .

The narrative is divided into sections controlled by different voices, often taking the form of specific written documents:

### 1\. The Journal of Brian Aspinwall
* **Role:** Frame Narrator / Teacher / Biographer. 
* **Format:** Diaries and Journals (1939–1947). 
* **Perspective:** Aspinwall represents the acolyte. A "moral fusspot" and aspiring divinity student who is physically unfit for military service, Aspinwall projects his need for a spiritual father onto Prescott . His journals record the day-to-day decline of the Rector and the operations of the school during World War II. Aspinwall is sophisticated enough to doubt his own objectivity, yet his "possessive admiration" often blinds him to the Rector's faults .

### 2\. The Memoirs of Horace Havistock
* **Role:** Prescott's Oldest Friend. 
* **Format:** Memoir titled "The Art of Friendship". 
* **Perspective:** Havistock provides the deep history. Having attended boarding school and Oxford with Prescott, he remembers "Frank" before he became "The Rector" . Havistock's account humanizes Prescott, revealing the insecurities and the "single-minded ambition" that drove an orphaned boy to build an empire . His tone is one of affectionate but clear-eyed detachment; he knows where the bodies are buried .

### 3\. The Notes of David Griscam
* **Role:** Chairman of the Board of Trustees / Alumnus (Class of 1890s). 
* **Format:** Notes and Recollections. 
* **Perspective:** Griscam offers the institutional view. A "white-shoe lawyer," he manages the financial and legal machinery that sustains Justin . His relationship with Prescott is fraught with ambivalence; he "both idolizes and dislikes" the man . Griscam is burdened by his own family shame—his father committed suicide after being exposed as a swindler—and he looks to Prescott for validation . His narrative reveals the ruthlessness required to keep the school afloat and the personal cost paid by his own son, Jules .

### 4\. The Story of Cordelia Prescott Turnbull
* **Role:** The Rector's Daughter. 
* **Format:** Interview / Oral History. 
* **Perspective:** Cordelia is the voice of domestic collateral damage. The youngest of three daughters, she describes herself as the "rebel" . Her account strips away the Great Man's public persona to reveal a father who was distant, controlling, and willing to sacrifice his family's happiness for the sake of his institution . Her narrative is essential for understanding the patriarchal tyranny that undergirds the school's philosophy.

### 5\. The Manuscript of Charley Strong
* **Role:** Alumnus / Cordelia's Fiancé. 
* **Format:** Manuscript / Letters. 
* **Perspective:** Charley Strong represents the "perfect" Justin boy who is ultimately crushed by the Rector's love . A brilliant but physically frail young man suffering from tuberculosis, Charley becomes the battleground between Cordelia and her father. His narrative details how Prescott manipulated his life, ostensibly to "save" him from a marriage that might kill him, but in reality to maintain control over his favorite disciple .

### 6\. The Memoir of Jules Griscam
* **Role:** Rebellious Student / Son of David Griscam. 
* **Format:** Memoir / Anecdotes. 
* **Perspective:** Jules is the anti-Aspinwall. Cynical, clever, and openly hostile to the "Justin spirit," he sees Prescott as a fraud and a performer . His narrative chronicles his calculated rebellion against the school's authoritarianism, culminating in his expulsion and subsequent self-destruction . Jules's perspective provides the most direct challenge to the Rector's moral authority.

## Plot Summary
The novel's plot is non-linear, moving back and forth in time as Aspinwall reads documents or interviews subjects. However, the chronological arc of Francis Prescott's life can be reconstructed to understand the trajectory of the "Justin" experiment.

### Early Life and Inspiration (1860s–1880s)
Francis Prescott is born in New England around 1860\. His early life is marked by loss: his father is killed in the Civil War, and his mother dies of disease shortly thereafter, leaving him an orphan . This trauma instills in him a fierce self-reliance and a need for structure. He attends a boarding school where he meets Horace Havistock. Even as a youth, Prescott is an "introvert and an all-round achiever," displaying a magnetic intensity that draws others to him .

Prescott continues his education at Oxford University in England. It is here that he encounters the British public school system (such as Eton and Harrow) and is inspired to transplant this model to the United States . He envisions a school that combines British academic rigor with American democratic ideals (though the school ultimately becomes a bastion of elitism) . Returning to America in 1881, he works briefly for a railroad—a period that grounds him in the realities of American industry—before entering the ministry . He marries Harriet Winslow, a woman of impeccable Boston lineage, whose social standing and stoicism will prove essential to the founding of Justin Martyr .

### The Founding and Rise of Justin (1890s–1920s)
Justin Martyr Academy is founded with the specific aim of molding "perfect Christian gentlemen" . Prescott's leadership style is established early on: he is an absolute monarch. He believes in a "muscular Christianity," emphasizing physical toughness, moral absolutism, and rigorous discipline .

David Griscam's narrative illuminates this era. Entering the school in 1891, Griscam is a sensitive boy carrying the weight of his father's financial crimes and suicide . Prescott becomes a surrogate father to Griscam, but the relationship is transactional; Prescott utilizes Griscam's legal mind and loyalty to secure the school's endowment and manage its board of trustees . Griscam's account reveals that the "miracle" of Justin was built not just on faith, but on shrewd maneuvering and the cultivation of wealthy patrons .

During this period, Prescott's domestic life suffers. His "single-minded ambition" to build the perfect school often takes him away from his wife and three daughters . The school consumes all the oxygen in the household, a fact that breeds resentment in his youngest daughter, Cordelia .

### The Tragedy of Charley Strong (1920s)
One of the most poignant episodes in the novel involves Charley Strong, a Golden Boy of Justin who represents the ideal of the scholar-athlete-saint. Charley, however, contracts tuberculosis. He and Cordelia fall in love and plan to marry, a union that offers Charley a chance at personal happiness away from the school's influence .

Prescott intervenes decisively and cruelly. Believing that the excitement of marriage and a secular life would be fatal to Charley's health—and perhaps more importantly, his spiritual state—Prescott "ingeniously engineers" their breakup . He convinces Charley that it is his "sad duty" to end the engagement. Charley returns to the school's infirmary, where he dies with his faith in Prescott restored, but Cordelia is left devastated and permanently estranged from her father . This incident epitomizes the Rector's willingness to sacrifice individual happiness for what he perceives as a higher moral good.

### The Rebellion of Jules Griscam (1930s)
As the 20th century progresses, the Victorian values of Justin Martyr begin to clash with the modern world. This conflict is personified in Jules Griscam, David Griscam's son. Unlike his father, Jules is not looking for a savior; he is looking for flaws. He detests the "Justin spirit" and mocks the Rector's pomposity .

Jules engages in a campaign of calculated subversion. The conflict escalates until Jules, in a drunken rage, drives back to the campus and throws a rock through the chapel window—a symbolic shattering of the school's sacred image . Prescott expels him immediately. The expulsion sets Jules on a nihilistic path; he is expelled from Harvard and eventually dies in a car accident in Europe, accompanied by a French mistress . The accident is hinted to be caused by his own "possibly deliberate recklessness" . To David Griscam, this is a tragedy; to Prescott, it is a confirmation that Jules lacked the moral fiber to survive .

### The Twilight of the Rector (1939–1947)
The novel's present-day action begins in 1939 with Brian Aspinwall's arrival. By this time, Prescott is a legend, but a fading one. The school is filled with whispers about his retirement. The outbreak of World War II further destabilizes the institution, as masters and boys leave for the front, and the certitudes of the 19th century seem increasingly irrelevant .

A crisis of succession emerges. The trustees appoint Duncan Moore as the new headmaster in 1941 . Moore is a modernist; he plans to relax the strict discipline, modernize the curriculum, and liberalize admissions to include students outside the traditional WASP circle . These proposed changes horrify the "old guard" of alumni and faculty, who view them as a desecration of Prescott's legacy.

In a moment of high drama, the octogenarian Prescott is tempted to lead a coup against his successor. He nearly "puts himself at the head of this rebellious old guard" . However, Brian Aspinwall, who has come to understand the necessity of change, alerts David Griscam. Griscam intervenes, persuading Prescott that destroying his successor would ultimately destroy the school he built . Prescott stands down, accepting his obsolescence.

The novel concludes with Prescott's death. In his final years, he is depicted as a man who has outlived his era but retained his dignity. Aspinwall, reflecting on his biography, realizes that the truth of Francis Prescott lies somewhere between the monster and the saint, a man who "learned the real tragedy of living too long... is losing one's dignity" .

## Characters
The characters in *The Rector of Justin* serve as distinct archetypes within the ecosystem of the American boarding school, each representing a different response to the Rector's authority.

### Francis "Frank" Prescott
* **Archetype:** The Flawed Titan. 
* **Analysis:** Prescott is a "personification of 20th-century New England" . He combines the intellectual rigor of a scholar with the ruthless pragmatism of a CEO. His theology is one of action rather than contemplation; he believes in "doing" rather than "being" . However, his strength is also his weakness. His inability to delegate, his need for total control, and his tendency to "play God" alienate his family and destroy fragile students like Charley Strong. As Auchincloss writes, he is "part authoritarian martinet, part moral fusspot," yet tempered by a genuine, if terrifying, Christian faith . 
* **Key Quote:** "I was sophisticated enough to know that the written word is no mirror of the writer's character... while the professional, a monster of ego, can convince you in a phrase that he has the innocence of a child." .

### Brian Aspinwall
* **Archetype:** The Disciple / The Witness. 
* **Analysis:** Aspinwall is the conduit for the reader's judgment. His initial timidity evolves into a quiet strength. He is the only character who truly loves Prescott without wanting something from him (unlike Griscam) or hating him (unlike Jules) . His decision to enter the ministry and his eventual role in saving the school's transition to Duncan Moore demonstrate that he has internalized the best of Prescott's teachings while rejecting his stubbornness .

### David Griscam
* **Archetype:** The Kingmaker. 
* **Analysis:** Griscam represents the marriage of Capital and Church. He is the "white-shoe lawyer" who ensures the school has the funds to operate . His tragedy is the realization that his devotion to Prescott came at the expense of his relationship with his son, Jules. He "enters Justin in 1891, burdened with the knowledge that his father has ended his life a swindler," and spends his life trying to erase that stain through service to the school .

### Cordelia Prescott Turnbull
* **Archetype:** The Electra Figure. 
* **Analysis:** Cordelia's narrative provides the necessary feminist critique of the "Great Man" theory. She exposes the domestic vacuum created by Prescott's ambition. Her bitterness is not just teenage rebellion but a deep-seated reaction to emotional neglect. She is the "rebel in the family" who sees her father not as a saint, but as a man who stole her lover (Charley Strong) and ruined her life .

### Jules Griscam
* **Archetype:** The Nihilist / The Modern Rebel. 
* **Analysis:** Jules is the "Lucifer" to Prescott's "God." He challenges the very premises of the school: that authority is benevolent and that tradition has value. His rebellion is destructive, yet it highlights the school's inability to accommodate difference or dissent. His death is the ultimate proof that there is no place for the non-conformist in Prescott's world .

### Horace Havistock
* **Archetype:** The Memory Keeper. 
* **Analysis:** Havistock serves to anchor Prescott in reality. He remembers the boy before the myth. His memoir, "The Art of Friendship," suggests that his life's work has been the observation of his friend, a role that is both touching and slightly pathetic . He provides the context of the "old Boston" world that birthed them both .

## Themes
The novel is rich in thematic complexity, using the microcosm of the boarding school to explore broader societal issues.

### The Collapse of Aristocratic Values
*The Rector of Justin* chronicles the decline of the WASP elite. Prescott's school is founded on the assumption that a specific class of Protestant men is destined to lead the nation in government, finance, and the church . The novel tracks the erosion of this confidence. By the end of the narrative, the "socially exclusive" nature of the school is being challenged by the "rising middle class" and a more meritocratic, diverse America . The transition from Prescott to Duncan Moore symbolizes the shift from "aristocratic values" to modern, liberal pragmatism .

### Moral Ambiguity and the "Great Man"
Auchincloss refuses to canonize or condemn Prescott. The novel asks whether great achievements necessarily require great ruthlessness. Prescott molds generations of leaders, but he also destroys individuals who do not fit his mold. The novel explores the "internal contradictions and self-delusion" required to maintain such absolute authority . As *The Saturday Review* noted, Auchincloss provides a "double view" of his characters, where they can be "morally monstrous" yet historically significant .

### The Tension Between Tradition and Progress
The conflict between the "old guard" and the new administration of Duncan Moore is a central tension. The novel posits that institutions like Justin Martyr must evolve to survive. Prescott's initial resistance to Moore's "mild relaxation of discipline" and "changes of curriculum" reflects the fear that modernization equals degradation . However, the novel ultimately endorses the necessity of change, as even Prescott is persuaded to let the new order take over .

### Fathers and Sons (Literal and Surrogate)
The novel is obsessed with paternity. Prescott is the "father" of the school and a surrogate father to Aspinwall and David Griscam. However, he is a failure as a biological father to his daughters. The relationships between biological fathers and sons (David and Jules Griscam) are fraught with disappointment and tragedy, while the surrogate relationships (Prescott and Aspinwall) are more successful but still complex. This theme echoes the "muscular Christian" ideal where spiritual lineage often superseded biological ties .

## Background and Inspirations
### The Groton School and Endicott Peabody
It is widely acknowledged that *The Rector of Justin* is based on the Groton School and its legendary headmaster, Endicott Peabody .

* **Parallels:** Like the fictional Justin Martyr, Groton was founded in the 1880s (1884) to educate the American elite . Endicott Peabody, like Prescott, was educated in England (Cheltenham and Cambridge), was physically imposing ("fair, athletic, pious"), and ran his school with autocratic zeal until his retirement in 1940 . Peabody was known as "The Rector," a title Auchincloss uses for Prescott, although in the novel, the school is officially named Justin Martyr . 
* **Divergences:** Auchincloss, a Groton alumnus (Class of 1935), was careful to obscure some direct connections. He claimed in interviews that Prescott was actually modeled on Learned Hand, a famous federal judge and intellectual, to capture the character's specific brand of "erudite" bullying . He noted that this disclaimer was partly to "placate Peabody's admirers," including his own father .

### Real-Life Figures in the Narrative
* **Brian Aspinwall:** Modeled on **Malcolm Strachan**, a real-life English teacher at Groton who was a close confidant of Peabody and a devout Christian. Like Aspinwall, Strachan had considered writing a novel about the Rector's theology . 
* **The School Environment:** The descriptions of "icy morning showers," "small cubicles with no privacy," and the emphasis on "perfect Christian gentlemen" are drawn directly from Auchincloss's own "miserable" and "brutal" experiences at Groton .

## Critical Reception
Upon its publication in 1964, *The Rector of Justin* was a major literary event.

### Contemporary Reviews
* ***The New York Times:*** Orville Prescott (no relation to the character) praised the novel's characterization, noting that "by a happy chance and a familiar literary convention, the six observers are all expert novelists" . The review highlighted the novel's subtlety and the effectiveness of its multi-narrator structure. 
* ***Harper's Magazine:*** In a famous blurb, the magazine called the book "almost certainly the finest work ever written about an American preparatory school" . 
* ***The Saturday Review:*** Granville Hicks reviewed the book positively on July 11, 1964, discussing the "double view" Auchincloss provides of his characters . 
* **Negative Criticism:** *The New York Review of Books*, reflecting the shifting literary tides of the 1960s, panned the novel. Critic Robert M. Adams called it "fake criticism," arguing that it was "afraid to ask the questions that hurt" and was too comfortable within the elite world it purported to analyze .

### Commercial Success
The novel was a commercial blockbuster. It topped *The New York Times* Best Seller list and remained a contender for thirty-five weeks . It was the \#6 best-selling novel of the entire year in 1964, competing with titles like John le Carré's *The Spy Who Came in from the Cold* and Saul Bellow's *Herzog*.24

### Awards and Honors
The novel's reception culminated in nominations for the most prestigious awards in American literature:

* **National Book Award (1965):** Finalist for Fiction. It lost to Saul Bellow's *Herzog*.1 
* **Pulitzer Prize (1965):** Finalist for Fiction. It lost to Shirley Ann Grau's *The Keepers of the House*.1

The loss to *Herzog* is often interpreted by literary historians as a symbolic "passing of the torch" from the WASP-centric "society novel" to the Jewish-American literary voice that would dominate the late 1960s and 1970s .

## Literary Significance and Legacy
*The Rector of Justin* remains Louis Auchincloss's most famous and enduring work. It is considered a cornerstone of the "boarding school" genre, influencing later works like *A Separate Peace* and *Dead Poets Society* (though it predates the film) .

The novel's legacy lies in its precise, almost anthropological documentation of a specific American subculture before its decline. As noted by critics, Auchincloss serves as the bridge between the world of Henry James/Edith Wharton and the modern era . While he was often criticized in later years for sticking to the "tiny sliver" of upper-crust society, *The Rector of Justin* is defended as a universal story of ambition and human fallibility, transcending its setting to ask fundamental questions about how we educate the young and how we remember the old .

In 2000, the significance of Auchincloss's body of work, with *The Rector of Justin* at its center, was recognized when he was named a "Living Landmark" by the New York Landmarks Conservancy . The novel continues to be cited as the definitive fictional account of the American prep school experience .

Griscam is burdened by his own family shame—his father committed suicide after being exposed as a swindler—and he looks to Prescott for validation.
His narrative reveals the ruthlessness required to keep the school afloat and the personal cost paid by his own son, Jules.
Cordelia Prescott Turnbull's role is The Rector's Daughter.
Cordelia Prescott Turnbull's format is Interview / Oral History.
Cordelia is the voice of domestic collateral damage.
The youngest of three daughters, she describes herself as the "rebel".
Her account strips away the Great Man's public persona to reveal a father who was distant, controlling, and willing to sacrifice his family's happiness for the sake of his institution.
Her narrative is essential for understanding the patriarchal tyranny that undergirds the school's philosophy.
Charley Strong's role is Alumnus / Cordelia's Fiancé.
Charley Strong's format is Manuscript / Letters.
Charley Strong represents the "perfect" Justin boy who is ultimately crushed by the Rector's love.
A brilliant but physically frail young man suffering from tuberculosis, Charley becomes the battleground between Cordelia and her father.
His narrative details how Prescott manipulated his life, ostensibly to "save" him from a marriage that might kill him, but in reality to maintain control over his favorite disciple.
Jules Griscam's role is Rebellious Student / Son of David Griscam.
Jules Griscam's format is Memoir / Anecdotes.
Jules is the anti-Aspinwall.
Cynical, clever, and openly hostile to the "Justin spirit," he sees Prescott as a fraud and a performer.
His narrative chronicles his calculated rebellion against the school's authoritarianism, culminating in his expulsion and subsequent self-destruction.
Jules's perspective provides the most direct challenge to the Rector's moral authority.
The novel's plot is non-linear, moving back and forth in time as Aspinwall reads documents or interviews subjects.
The chronological arc of Francis Prescott's life can be reconstructed to understand the trajectory of the "Justin" experiment.
Francis Prescott is born in New England around 1860.
His early life is marked by loss: his father is killed in the Civil War, and his mother dies of disease shortly thereafter, leaving him an orphan.
This trauma instills in him a fierce self-reliance and a need for structure.
He attends a boarding school where he meets Horace Havistock.
Even as a youth, Prescott is an "introvert and an all-round achiever," displaying a magnetic intensity that draws others to him.
Prescott continues his education at Oxford University in England.
It is here that he encounters the British public school system (such as Eton and Harrow) and is inspired to transplant this model to the United States.
He envisions a school that combines British academic rigor with American democratic ideals (though the school ultimately becomes a bastion of elitism).
Returning to America in 1881, he works briefly for a railroad—a period that grounds him in the realities of American industry—before entering the ministry.
He marries Harriet Winslow, a woman of impeccable Boston lineage, whose social standing and stoicism will prove essential to the founding of Justin Martyr.
Justin Martyr Academy is founded with the specific aim of molding "perfect Christian gentlemen".
Prescott's leadership style is established early on: he is an absolute monarch.
He believes in a "muscular Christianity," emphasizing physical toughness, moral absolutism, and rigorous discipline.
David Griscam's narrative illuminates this era.
Entering the school in 1891, Griscam is a sensitive boy carrying the weight of his father's financial crimes and suicide.
Prescott becomes a surrogate father to Griscam, but the relationship is transactional.
Prescott utilizes Griscam's legal mind and loyalty to secure the school's endowment and manage its board of trustees.
Griscam's account reveals that the "miracle" of Justin was built not just on faith, but on shrewd maneuvering and the cultivation of wealthy patrons.
During this period, Prescott's domestic life suffers.
His "single-minded ambition" to build the perfect school often takes him away from his wife and three daughters.
The school consumes all the oxygen in the household, a fact that breeds resentment in his youngest daughter, Cordelia.
One of the most poignant episodes in the novel involves Charley Strong, a Golden Boy of Justin who represents the ideal of the scholar-athlete-saint.
Charley contracts tuberculosis.
He and Cordelia fall in love and plan to marry, a union that offers Charley a chance at personal happiness away from the school's influence.
Prescott intervenes decisively and cruelly.
Believing that the excitement of marriage and a secular life would be fatal to Charley's health—and perhaps more importantly, his spiritual state—Prescott "ingeniously engineers" their breakup.
He convinces Charley that it is his "sad duty" to end the engagement.
Charley returns to the school's infirmary, where he dies with his faith in Prescott restored, but Cordelia is left devastated and permanently estranged from her father.
This incident epitomizes the Rector's willingness to sacrifice individual happiness for what he perceives as a higher moral good.
As the 20th century progresses, the Victorian values of Justin Martyr begin to clash with the modern world.
This conflict is personified in Jules Griscam, David Griscam's son.
Unlike his father, Jules is not looking for a savior; he is looking for flaws.
He detests the "Justin spirit" and mocks the Rector's pomposity.
Jules engages in a campaign of calculated subversion.
The conflict escalates until Jules, in a drunken rage, drives back to the campus and throws a rock through the chapel window—a symbolic shattering of the school's sacred image.
Prescott expels him immediately.
The expulsion sets Jules on a nihilistic path; he is expelled from Harvard and eventually dies in a car accident in Europe, accompanied by a French mistress.
The accident is hinted to be caused by his own "possibly deliberate recklessness".
To David Griscam, this is a tragedy; to Prescott, it is a confirmation that Jules lacked the moral fiber to survive.
The novel's present-day action begins in 1939 with Brian Aspinwall's arrival.
By this time, Prescott is a legend, but a fading one.
The school is filled with whispers about his retirement.
The outbreak of World War II further destabilizes the institution, as masters and boys leave for the front, and the certitudes of the 19th century seem increasingly irrelevant.
A crisis of succession emerges.
The trustees appoint Duncan Moore as the new headmaster in 1941.
Moore is a modernist; he plans to relax the strict discipline, modernize the curriculum, and liberalize admissions to include students outside the traditional WASP circle.
These proposed changes horrify the "old guard" of alumni and faculty, who view them as a desecration of Prescott's legacy.
In a moment of high drama, the octogenarian Prescott is tempted to lead a coup against his successor.
He nearly "puts himself at the head of this rebellious old guard".
However, Brian Aspinwall, who has come to understand the necessity of change, alerts David Griscam.
Griscam intervenes, persuading Prescott that destroying his successor would ultimately destroy the school he built.
Prescott stands down, accepting his obsolescence.
The novel concludes with Prescott's death.
In his final years, he is depicted as a man who has outlived his era but retained his dignity.

Aspinwall, reflecting on his biography, realizes that the truth of Francis Prescott lies somewhere between the monster and the saint, a man who "learned the real tragedy of living too long... is losing one's dignity".
The characters in *The Rector of Justin* serve as distinct archetypes within the ecosystem of the American boarding school, each representing a different response to the Rector's authority.
Prescott is a "personification of 20th-century New England".
He combines the intellectual rigor of a scholar with the ruthless pragmatism of a CEO.
His theology is one of action rather than contemplation; he believes in "doing" rather than "being".
His strength is also his weakness.
His inability to delegate, his need for total control, and his tendency to "play God" alienate his family and destroy fragile students like Charley Strong.
As Auchincloss writes, he is "part authoritarian martinet, part moral fusspot," yet tempered by a genuine, if terrifying, Christian faith.
Aspinwall is the conduit for the reader's judgment.
His initial timidity evolves into a quiet strength.
He is the only character who truly loves Prescott without wanting something from him (unlike Griscam) or hating him (unlike Jules).

His decision to enter the ministry and his eventual role in saving the school's transition to Duncan Moore demonstrate that he has internalized the best of Prescott's teachings while rejecting his stubbornness.
Griscam represents the marriage of Capital and Church.
He is the "white-shoe lawyer" who ensures the school has the funds to operate.
His tragedy is the realization that his devotion to Prescott came at the expense of his relationship with his son, Jules.
He "enters Justin in 1891, burdened with the knowledge that his father has ended his life a swindler," and spends his life trying to erase that stain through service to the school.
Cordelia's narrative provides the necessary feminist critique of the "Great Man" theory.
She exposes the domestic vacuum created by Prescott's ambition.
Her bitterness is not just teenage rebellion but a deep-seated reaction to emotional neglect.
She is the "rebel in the family" who sees her father not as a saint, but as a man who stole her lover (Charley Strong) and ruined her life.
Jules is the "Lucifer" to Prescott's "God."
He challenges the very premises of the school: that authority is benevolent and that tradition has value.
His rebellion is destructive, yet it highlights the school's inability to accommodate difference or dissent.
His death is the ultimate proof that there is no place for the non-conformist in Prescott's world.
Havistock serves to anchor Prescott in reality.
He remembers the boy before the myth.
His memoir, "The Art of Friendship," suggests that his life's work has been the observation of his friend, a role that is both touching and slightly pathetic.
He provides the context of the "old Boston" world that birthed them both.
The novel is rich in thematic complexity, using the microcosm of the boarding school to explore broader societal issues.
*The Rector of Justin* chronicles the decline of the WASP elite.
Prescott's school is founded on the assumption that a specific class of Protestant men is destined to lead the nation in government, finance, and the church.
The novel tracks the erosion of this confidence.
By the end of the narrative, the "socially exclusive" nature of the school is being challenged by the "rising middle class" and a more meritocratic, diverse America.
The transition from Prescott to Duncan Moore symbolizes the shift from "aristocratic values" to modern, liberal pragmatism.
Auchincloss refuses to canonize or condemn Prescott.
The novel asks whether great achievements necessarily require great ruthlessness.
Prescott molds generations of leaders, but he also destroys individuals who do not fit his mold.
The novel explores the "internal contradictions and self-delusion" required to maintain such absolute authority.
As *The Saturday Review* noted, Auchincloss provides a "double view" of his characters, where they can be "morally monstrous" yet historically significant.
The conflict between the "old guard" and the new administration of Duncan Moore is a central tension.
The novel posits that institutions like Justin Martyr must evolve to survive.
Prescott's initial resistance to Moore's "mild relaxation of discipline" and "changes of curriculum" reflects the fear that modernization equals degradation.
However, the novel ultimately endorses the necessity of change, as even Prescott is persuaded to let the new order take over.
The novel is obsessed with paternity.
Prescott is the "father" of the school and a surrogate father to Aspinwall and David Griscam.
However, he is a failure as a biological father to his daughters.

The relationships between biological fathers and sons (David and Jules Griscam) are fraught with disappointment and tragedy, while the surrogate relationships (Prescott and Aspinwall) are more successful but still complex.
This theme echoes the "muscular Christian" ideal where spiritual lineage often superseded biological ties.
It is widely acknowledged that *The Rector of Justin* is based on the Groton School and its legendary headmaster, Endicott Peabody.
Like the fictional Justin Martyr, Groton was founded in the 1880s (1884) to educate the American elite.

Endicott Peabody, like Prescott, was educated in England (Cheltenham and Cambridge), was physically imposing ("fair, athletic, pious"), and ran his school with autocratic zeal until his retirement in 1940.
Peabody was known as "The Rector," a title Auchincloss uses for Prescott, although in the novel, the school is officially named Justin Martyr.
Auchincloss, a Groton alumnus (Class of 1935), was careful to obscure some direct connections.
He claimed in interviews that Prescott was actually modeled on Learned Hand, a famous federal judge and intellectual, to capture the character's specific brand of "erudite" bullying.
He noted that this disclaimer was partly to "placate Peabody's admirers," including his own father.
Brian Aspinwall is modeled on Malcolm Strachan, a real-life English teacher at Groton who was a close confidant of Peabody and a devout Christian.
Like Aspinwall, Strachan had considered writing a novel about the Rector's theology.

The descriptions of "icy morning showers," "small cubicles with no privacy," and the emphasis on "perfect Christian gentlemen" are drawn directly from Auchincloss's own "miserable" and "brutal" experiences at Groton.
Upon its publication in 1964, *The Rector of Justin* was a major literary event.
Orville Prescott (no relation to the character) praised the novel's characterization, noting that "by a happy chance and a familiar literary convention, the six observers are all expert novelists".
The review highlighted the novel's subtlety and the effectiveness of its multi-narrator structure.
In a famous blurb, *Harper's Magazine* called the book "almost certainly the finest work ever written about an American preparatory school".
Granville Hicks reviewed the book positively on July 11, 1964, discussing the "double view" Auchincloss provides of his characters.
*The New York Review of Books*, reflecting the shifting literary tides of the 1960s, panned the novel.
Critic Robert M. Adams called it "fake criticism," arguing that it was "afraid to ask the questions that hurt" and was too comfortable within the elite world it purported to analyze.
The novel was a commercial blockbuster.
It topped *The New York Times* Best Seller list and remained a contender for thirty-five weeks.
It was the #6 best-selling novel of the entire year in 1964, competing with titles like John le Carré's *The Spy Who Came in from the Cold* and Saul Bellow's *Herzog*.
The novel's reception culminated in nominations for the most prestigious awards in American literature.
*The Rector of Justin* was a Finalist for Fiction in the National Book Award (1965).
It lost to Saul Bellow's *Herzog*.
*The Rector of Justin* was a Finalist for Fiction in the Pulitzer Prize (1965).
It lost to Shirley Ann Grau's *The Keepers of the House*.

The loss to *Herzog* is often interpreted by literary historians as a symbolic "passing of the torch" from the WASP-centric "society novel" to the Jewish-American literary voice that would dominate the late 1960s and 1970s.
*The Rector of Justin* remains Louis Auchincloss's most famous and enduring work.
It is considered a cornerstone of the "boarding school" genre, influencing later works like *A Separate Peace* and *Dead Poets Society* (though it predates the film).
The novel's legacy lies in its precise, almost anthropological documentation of a specific American subculture before its decline.
As noted by critics, Auchincloss serves as the bridge between the world of Henry James/Edith Wharton and the modern era.

While he was often criticized in later years for sticking to the "tiny sliver" of upper-crust society, *The Rector of Justin* is defended as a universal story of ambition and human fallibility, transcending its setting to ask fundamental questions about how we educate the young and how we remember the old.
In 2000, the significance of Auchincloss's body of work, with *The Rector of Justin* at its center, was recognized when he was named a "Living Landmark" by the New York Landmarks Conservancy.
The novel continues to be cited as the definitive fictional account of the American prep school experience.

1.title: The Rector of Justin
1.content:
The Rector of Justin [![Image 1: Photo of the original front cover](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/8/8a/The_Rector_of_Justin_1964_hardcover_dust_jacket.png/250px-The_Rector_of_Justin_1964_hardcover_dust_jacket.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:The_Rector_of_Justin_1964_hardcover_dust_jacket.png "Photo of the original front cover")
Cover of the 1964 first edition
Author[Louis Auchincloss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_Auchincloss "Louis Auchincloss")
Language English
Genre[Psychological fiction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psychological_fiction "Psychological fiction")
Publisher[Houghton Mifflin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houghton_Mifflin "Houghton Mifflin")
Publication date 1964
[ISBN](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ISBN_(identifier) "ISBN (identifier)")[978-0-618-22489-0](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special:BookSources/978-0-618-22489-0 "Special:BookSources/978-0-618-22489-0")

_**The Rector of Justin**_ is a 1964 [psychological fiction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psychological_fiction "Psychological fiction") novel by [Louis Auchincloss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_Auchincloss "Louis Auchincloss") about the headmaster (or "[rector](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rector_(ecclesiastical) "Rector (ecclesiastical)")") of a socially exclusive American [boarding school](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boarding_school "Boarding school"). Over the decades, various narrators provide contrasting perspectives on rector Francis Prescott's charismatic personality and autocratic leadership style. Through the narrators' disagreements, the novel gradually unveils that [White Anglo-Saxon Protestant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Anglo-Saxon_Protestants "White Anglo-Saxon Protestants") society—of which Prescott is a reluctant mascot—has lost its innocence and abandoned its Christian values.

The novel was a commercial hit and was warmly received by most contemporary critics. It was a finalist for the [Pulitzer Prize for Fiction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pulitzer_Prize_for_Fiction "Pulitzer Prize for Fiction") and the [National Book Award for Fiction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Book_Award_for_Fiction "National Book Award for Fiction"), losing to [Shirley Ann Grau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shirley_Ann_Grau "Shirley Ann Grau")'s _[The Keeper of the House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Keepers\_of\_the\_House "The Keepers of the House")_ and [Saul Bellow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saul_Bellow "Saul Bellow")'s _[Herzog](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herzog\_(novel) "Herzog (novel)")_, respectively. Its loss to _Herzog_ marked [American literary fiction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_literature#Post-World_War_II_fiction "American literature")'s transition from realist [society novels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Society_novel "Society novel") about the [American upper class](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_upper_class "American upper class") to poetic prose, [avant-garde style](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avant-garde_literature "Avant-garde literature"), and culturally diverse protagonists.

Upon its release, _[Harper's Magazine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harper%27s\_Magazine "Harper's Magazine")_ called the book "almost certainly the finest work ever written about an American [preparatory school](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/College-preparatory_school "College-preparatory school")". It is often considered Auchincloss' greatest novel.

The story is told through six narrators: [frame narrator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frame_story "Frame story") Brian Aspinwall, a teacher at Massachusetts [Episcopal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Episcopal_Church_(United_States) "Episcopal Church (United States)") boarding school Justin Martyr ("Justin" for short; named for [the Christian figure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Justin_Martyr "Justin Martyr")), who is asked to write a biography of its founder Francis Prescott; and writings and interviews from five people who knew him.

In 1939, Aspinwall begins teaching English at Justin. Prescott's contradictions fascinate him. Prescott is an intellectual, but Justin is laddish and focused on sports. Prescott's oldest friend Horace Havistock is gay, but Justin is institutionally homophobic. The school claims to be more democratic than its peers, but its students are generally rich. After the [Fall of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_of_France "Fall of France"), Havistock persuades Prescott to retire, arguing that their shared world is dying.

Havistock and Prescott went to boarding school together.[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Rector_of_Justin#cite_note-3) A [Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Civil_War "American Civil War") orphan whose family was respectable but not especially wealthy, Prescott resents rich boys like Havistock, who become targets for his cruel wit. Even so, Havistock befriends him. Prescott dreams of building a different kind of boarding school, focused on religious and [civic virtue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civic_virtue "Civic virtue"). He has a crisis of faith at [Oxford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Oxford "University of Oxford"), but reconverts to Christianity after experiencing a vision of his dead father. Havistock persuades his friend Eliza to break off her engagement with the re-energized Prescott, who will always put his career over his relationships.

The chairman of the Justin board, [white-shoe lawyer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White-shoe_firm "White-shoe firm") David Griscam, both idolizes and dislikes Prescott. He appreciated Justin's family atmosphere, but admits that Justin's bullying and [code of silence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Code_of_silence "Code of silence") taught him to be "underhanded". Neither Griscam nor his wife share Prescott's Episcopal faith: Griscam is [agnostic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agnosticism "Agnosticism"), while his wife, an [evangelical Christian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evangelical_Christian "Evangelical Christian"), resents Justin's religious elitism. Griscam insists on sending his two sons to Justin anyway, but neither succeeds there.

Appealing to Prescott's ambition, Griscam encourages Prescott to solicit donations from men whose wealth he resents. Prescott wants to expel a donor's son for [academic dishonesty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academic_dishonesty "Academic dishonesty"), but Max Totten, a cynical [scholarship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scholarship "Scholarship") student, agrees to take the blame in exchange for a job at the donor's company. Although Max is expelled, he eventually takes over the family business and becomes one of Griscam's "most valued clients", while the son falls into alcoholism.

### Cordelia Prescott Turnbull

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Rector_of_Justin&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Cordelia Prescott Turnbull")]

Prescott's daughter Cordelia claims that Prescott started a boys' school due to his own repressed homosexual tendencies. She marries a Catholic to annoy him, but after Prescott gives his approval, she leaves her husband and moves to Paris, where she and her lover Charley Strong (a Justinian who loses his Christian faith in [World War I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_I "World War I")) become part of the [Lost Generation of American expatriates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lost_Generation#In_literature "Lost Generation"). Her mother visits her in Paris and reveals a deep intelligence that was repressed at Justin. Before Strong's death, Prescott reconverts him to Christianity, infuriating Cordelia. She returns to America and marries vulgar businessman Guy Turnbull, but surprisingly, Turnbull befriends Prescott, who craves his respect as a businessman and is impressed by his shameless materialism. Cordelia divorces Turnbull. Prescott confides to Aspinwall that while he has loved his daughters inadequately, he has shown them devotion.

In the last surviving chapter of a manuscript that Strong burned before his death, Strong recounts his hero worship of Prescott, which may be rooted in Prescott forgiving him for an early sexual indiscretion. He sees Prescott's Christian discipline as an alternative to the rootlessness of the Lost Generation.

In a memoir written before his death, David Griscam's son Jules implies that his father sent him to Justin because David worried that his materialism would spoil his children. Jules is a poor fit for Justin and Prescott eventually expels him for lying, but David gets Jules into [Harvard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvard_University "Harvard University") anyway. Jules concludes that "an act of desecration" is the only real way to get back at Prescott. He vandalizes several school relics and is arrested.[[b]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Rector_of_Justin#cite_note-7) When Prescott visits him in jail, Jules claims that Prescott uses religion to aggrandize himself, which wounds Prescott deeply. Jules drunkenly commits suicide, taking his lover with him.

After Prescott's successor softens religious discipline and accommodates practicing Catholics,[[c]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Rector_of_Justin#cite_note-9) Prescott plots to oust him. Aspinwall dislikes David Griscam's combination of materialism and tightfistedness, but tips him off anyway. Griscam persuades Prescott to relent by introducing him to elitist and racist dissidents on the Justin board, showing that his successor is the lesser of two evils. Prescott bitterly remarks that Justin is no different from any other prep school. He dies of cancer eight months later. Aspinwall resolves to finish his Prescott biography, although he implies that to preserve the idealized memory of Prescott, it will be "in some part [a] work[] of fiction".

[![Image 2: Refer to caption](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/cc/Louis_Auchincloss_with_President_Bush.jpg/250px-Louis_Auchincloss_with_President_Bush.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Louis_Auchincloss_with_President_Bush.jpg)

Author [Louis Auchincloss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_Auchincloss "Louis Auchincloss")**(center)** received the [National Medal of Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Medal_of_Arts "National Medal of Arts") in 2005. He stands between President [George W. Bush](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_W._Bush "George W. Bush") and First Lady [Laura Bush](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laura_Bush "Laura Bush").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Rector_of_Justin#cite_note-:0-10)

Louis Auchincloss was sent to his father's boarding school, [Groton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Groton_School "Groton School"), and graduated in 1935.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Rector_of_Justin#cite_note-:12-11) Although he later delivered the school's centennial address,[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Rector_of_Justin#cite_note-:13-12) he maintained a lifelong ambivalence for the institution, explaining that his first two years of prep school were a "festering misery"[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Rector_of_Justin#cite_note-:16-13) and that he was "at first abysmally wretched and later moderately content".[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Rector_of_Justin#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAuchincloss1969355-14) He got the idea for _The Rector of Justin_ from his high school English teacher, Malcolm Strachan,[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Rector_of_Justin#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAuchincloss197459-60-15) whose wife was the publisher of the _[Atlantic Monthly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlantic\_Monthly "Atlantic Monthly")_.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Rector_of_Justin#cite_note-16) Strachan had become a close confidant of Groton's founder and longtime headmaster, [Endicott Peabody](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endicott_Peabody_(educator) "Endicott Peabody (educator)"), and planned to write a novel showing that Peabody's "theology was subtler and more complicated than any of us supposed."[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Rector_of_Justin#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAuchincloss197460-17) After Strachan's premature death, Auchincloss resolved to write the novel his way.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Rector_of_Justin#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAuchincloss197460-17)

In 1960, Groton published a collection of essays from the school community to commemorate its 75th anniversary. In his essay, Auchincloss wrote that the alumni had many different impressions of their high school years, and speculated that the aging Peabody had been "troubled by the number of Grotons he seemed to have created and of how little any of them resembled his own."[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Rector_of_Justin#cite_note-:14-18) In addition, although published by the school, the essays voiced several criticisms of Groton. [Ellery Sedgwick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ellery_Sedgwick "Ellery Sedgwick") wrote that despite Groton's high-minded rhetoric, "evil and good have entered into Groton careers in a proportion astonishingly similar to their proportion in any community".[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Rector_of_Justin#cite_note-:4-19)[George Biddle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Biddle "George Biddle") said that while seven of his classmates were listed in _[Who's Who](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Who%27s\_Who "Who's Who")_, "nearly twice that number could, I suppose, be listed as absolute failures".[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Rector_of_Justin#cite_note-:5-20) Auchincloss later sent two of his three sons to Groton,[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Rector_of_Justin#cite_note-:16-13) although his biographer cautioned that, by that time, it was "a far more permissive place".[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Rector_of_Justin#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGelderman1993216-21)

Auchincloss had wanted to write a story about a boarding school headmaster for some time, although he was saving the idea "for [a] time when I should feel ready to handle it".[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Rector_of_Justin#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAuchincloss19684-22) In 1938, just three years after graduating from Groton, he drafted a novel in which a headmaster seeks to raise students "with the ideals of public service and a sense of [noblesse oblige](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noblesse_oblige "Noblesse oblige")", but realizes that he has failed, as most of his students chase lucrative jobs on Wall Street.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Rector_of_Justin#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPiket1989183-23)

Over time, Auchincloss decided that the story would need to cover a long span of time and that it would need to be either a biography or autobiography. He discarded the idea of an autobiography because a fictional Prescott would have trouble describing his effect on other people from his own perspective.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Rector_of_Justin#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAuchincloss19687-24) In 1956, Auchincloss published a predecessor of the story in _[Harper's Magazine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harper%27s\_Magazine "Harper's Magazine")_ under the title "The Trial of Mr. M."[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Rector_of_Justin#cite_note-25) The story details a retired boarding school headmaster who considers opposing his successor's reforms, but ultimately concedes that the school must adapt to the real world. Auchincloss recycles the imagery of the headmaster's lament—comparing himself to a vaudeville act in which a clown is "remorselessly" followed by a spotlight[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Rector_of_Justin#cite_note-26)—for Prescott's final monologue in the novel.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Rector_of_Justin#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPiket1989184-27)[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Rector_of_Justin#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDahl1986253-28)

In Auchincloss' first draft of the novel, David Griscam was the frame narrator instead of Brian Aspinwall, and the book emphasized the rivalry between Griscam and Prescott. He discarded the idea because Griscam's "personality got out of hand".[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Rector_of_Justin#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAuchincloss19688-29) He eventually came up with the idea of making the biographer a younger man who differed from Prescott in every way except their shared religious faith, which they both recognized was "almost totally lacking in the school, the faculty, the parents, and the trustees," who "care[d] only about the appearance of faith".[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Rector_of_Justin#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAuchincloss19688-29)

Late in his life, Auchincloss (who said that he had been sexually abused by another student in high school, without the school's knowledge[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Rector_of_Justin#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAuchincloss201063-64-30)) admitted that he had considered broaching the topic of [sexual abuse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sexual_abuse_in_primary_and_secondary_schools "Sexual abuse in primary and secondary schools") in _The Rector of Justin_, but ultimately left it out. He felt that the literary mores of the day would not permit him to address the matter with sufficient candor. He subsequently touched upon this theme in _The Scarlet Letters_ (2003) _and The Headmaster's Dilemma_ (2007), as well as his 2010 autobiography.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Rector_of_Justin#cite_note-31)

Auchincloss submitted a draft of the novel to [Houghton Mifflin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houghton_Mifflin_Harcourt "Houghton Mifflin Harcourt") in July 1963. It was published in July 1964.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Rector_of_Justin#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPiket1989181-32)

Auchincloss sought to build a composite narrative of the American boarding school between the [Gilded Age](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gilded_Age "Gilded Age") and [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II"), explaining that it was "the great era of headmasters". He reviewed a series of headmaster biographies from various schools, including Peabody's Groton, [St. Paul's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Paul%27s_School_(New_Hampshire) "St. Paul's School (New Hampshire)"), [St. Mark's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Mark%27s_School_(Massachusetts) "St. Mark's School (Massachusetts)"), and [Lawrenceville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lawrenceville_School "Lawrenceville School"), but dismissed them as "a dreary lot".[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Rector_of_Justin#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAuchincloss197435-33) Nonetheless, the novel frequently draws from Auchincloss' experiences at Groton in the 1930s. One critic quipped that in one scene, "the Rev. Francis Prescott, founder and first headmaster of Justin Martyr, an Episcopal school 30 miles west of Boston, was speaking about the Rev. Endicott Peabody, founder and first headmaster of Groton School, an Episcopal-oriented school 30 miles west of Boston".[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Rector_of_Justin#cite_note-:1-34)

The novel mirrors some of the compromises Peabody made to build Groton. According to one story, in 1891, Peabody financed Groton's main dormitory by allowing donors who contributed at least $5,000 (approximately $175,000 in 2025 dollars) to nominate one student for admission, notwithstanding the waiting list.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Rector_of_Justin#cite_note-35) He later remarked that focusing on educating wealthy students was "one of the great mistakes that [he] made as Headmaster".[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Rector_of_Justin#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAldred2017284-36) For his own part, Auchincloss commented that Peabody had no other option, since "who else in 1881 was going to support a new school started by three young men?"[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Rector_of_Justin#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAuchincloss197439-8)

[![Image 3: Photo of Endicott Peabody, Auchincloss' boarding school headmaster](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/08/Peabodyheadmaster.jpg/250px-Peabodyheadmaster.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Peabodyheadmaster.jpg)

[![Image 4: Photo of Learned Hand, an influential federal judge](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d4/LearnedHand1910a.jpg/250px-LearnedHand1910a.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:LearnedHand1910a.jpg)

The character of Frank Prescott was often compared to Endicott Peabody, although Auchincloss protested that the two men "shared not a single characteristic".[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Rector_of_Justin#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAuchincloss2010194-37) He explained that Peabody was "simple, straightforward, literal, and always sincere", while Prescott was "complex, arrogant, witty, cynical, intellectual", and "a bit of a charlatan".[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Rector_of_Justin#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAuchincloss197436-38) He admitted that he had borrowed "certain facts and dates" from Peabody's life, but maintained that Prescott was based, at least "in part", on federal judge [Learned Hand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Learned_Hand "Learned Hand"),[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Rector_of_Justin#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAuchincloss197460-17)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Rector_of_Justin#cite_note-:0-10) who he described as "the greatest man whom I ever had the good luck to know".[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Rector_of_Justin#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAuchincloss19685-39) However, he later recalled that [Archibald MacLeish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archibald_MacLeish "Archibald MacLeish") was the only person who recognized Hand's influence on Prescott.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Rector_of_Justin#cite_note-FOOTNOTEParsell198853-40)

Even so, upon its publication, the book reportedly "caused uproar among Groton alumni who saw it as an attack" on Peabody.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Rector_of_Justin#cite_note-41) Peabody's granddaughter [Marietta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marietta_Peabody_Tree "Marietta Peabody Tree") consoled Auchincloss by telling him that the criticism reflected how little his critics understood Peabody.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Rector_of_Justin#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGelderman1993155-42) In addition, Peabody's biographer Frank Ashburn commented that Frank Prescott "only remotely" resembled his subject,[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Rector_of_Justin#cite_note-:24-43) and [Larissa MacFarquhar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Larissa_MacFarquhar "Larissa MacFarquhar") wrote that "Prescott is a far more convoluted and ambiguous character" than Peabody.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Rector_of_Justin#cite_note-:13-12) One Groton graduate, [Cass Canfield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cass_Canfield "Cass Canfield") of the [Harper and Row](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harper_and_Row "Harper and Row") publishing house, publicly praised the book and Prescott's character in particular, but did not discuss the Peabody connection.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Rector_of_Justin#cite_note-44)[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Rector_of_Justin#cite_note-45)

Prescott's title (and thus the title of the book) also refers to Peabody. While Groton did not use the term "rector" for its headmaster (the term was instead used by [St. Paul's School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Paul%27s_School_(New_Hampshire) "St. Paul's School (New Hampshire)")), the school community informally referred to Endicott Peabody as "_the_ Rector".[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Rector_of_Justin#cite_note-46)

The character of Brian Aspinwall is modeled on Auchincloss' old mentor, Malcolm Strachan.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Rector_of_Justin#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAuchincloss197461-47) Auchincloss admitted that Aspinwall was "much weaker and less attractive ... than Malcolm had ever been", but rejected claims that the character was a veiled attack on Strachan.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Rector_of_Justin#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAuchincloss197461-47) He said that he wanted to make Aspinwall as different from Prescott as possible for dramatic effect.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Rector_of_Justin#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAuchincloss197460-17)

Auchincloss based Prescott's friend Horace Havistock on [University of Cambridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Cambridge "University of Cambridge") legal historian [G. T. Lapsley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/G._T._Lapsley "G. T. Lapsley").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Rector_of_Justin#cite_note-:12-11) Like Havistock, Lapsley was a gay man[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Rector_of_Justin#cite_note-48)[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Rector_of_Justin#cite_note-49) who left America for Europe.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Rector_of_Justin#cite_note-50)

Auchincloss spent most of his career detailing the decline of [White Anglo-Saxon Protestants](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Anglo-Saxon_Protestants "White Anglo-Saxon Protestants")' (WASPs) leading role in American society.[[d]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Rector_of_Justin#cite_note-52) Shortly before his death, he explained that while most of his WASP friends were _richer_ in the 21st century than they had been growing up, "everyone has moved up", and the old-money elite had "lost their monopoly."[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Rector_of_Justin#cite_note-:17-51)[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Rector_of_Justin#cite_note-:18-53) He added that "to have witnessed the disintegration of an economic ruling class in the 1930s from a front row seat ... was all a novelist could ask [for]."[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Rector_of_Justin#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGelderman1993167-54) In an early chapter of _The Rector of Justin_, Horace Havistock concedes that "the world of the private school" is necessarily tied up with "the world of personal honor and a Protestant God", and that "when a civilization crumbles, it crumbles all together."[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Rector_of_Justin#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAuchincloss196463-55)

### The collapse of aristocratic values

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Rector_of_Justin&action=edit&section=17 "Edit section: The collapse of aristocratic values")]

[![Image 5: Photo of Richard Whitney, a disgraced upper-class financier](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b8/Former_head_of_New_York_Stock_Exchange_before_Senate_Committee._Washington_D.C._Richard_Whitney%3B_former_President_of_the_New_York_Stock_Exchange%2C_was_the_first_witness_as_the_Senate_LCCN2016871192_%28cropped%29.jpg/250px-thumbnail.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Former_head_of_New_York_Stock_Exchange_before_Senate_Committee._Washington_D.C._Richard_Whitney;_former_President_of_the_New_York_Stock_Exchange,_was_the_first_witness_as_the_Senate_LCCN2016871192_(cropped).jpg)

The public disgrace of [Richard Whitney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Whitney_(financier) "Richard Whitney (financier)") (pictured), the aristocratic president of the [New York Stock Exchange](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_Stock_Exchange "New York Stock Exchange"), shocked upper-class society.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Rector_of_Justin#cite_note-:13-12)

_The Rector of Justin_ explores the erosion of the WASPs' self-belief that values instilled at schools like Groton entitled them to leadership roles in the corporate world and public service, and reflects Auchincloss' growing disillusionment with WASP society in the 1930s and 1940s. Auchincloss said that when he was growing up, the [Eastern Establishment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Establishment "Eastern Establishment") thought it "could be trusted to regulate itself".[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Rector_of_Justin#cite_note-:13-12) As an example of these values, the novel notes how after David Griscam's father went bankrupt and fled the country, his mother felt a "sacred duty" to pay off her absentee husband's debts, forcing the family to abandon its upper-class lifestyle.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Rector_of_Justin#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAuchincloss1964130-56) As a young man, Auchincloss resented the Groton-educated [Franklin Delano Roosevelt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franklin_Delano_Roosevelt "Franklin Delano Roosevelt")'s use of government to enforce morality in the corporate sphere, reasoning that it was a repudiation of Establishment values.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Rector_of_Justin#cite_note-:13-12) However, he eventually lost faith in the idea that WASPs were more moral than the general population. Another Groton alumnus, financier [Richard Whitney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Whitney_(financier) "Richard Whitney (financier)"), shocked high society with his 1938 [embezzlement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Embezzlement "Embezzlement") conviction;[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Rector_of_Justin#cite_note-:13-12) Auchincloss explored Whitney's misdeeds in his next novel, _The Embezzler_ (1966).[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Rector_of_Justin#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDahl1986125-57)

> Pa and Mother, of course, were supreme at Justin, but from the beginning we knew that Justin was not the real world. ... [A]lthough [the real world] treated Pa and Mother with respect, it was the kind of respect that people might pay to the sovereigns of a small Pacific Island kingdom, more exotic than powerful, not quite to be taken seriously, perhaps even a bit ridiculous.

Cordelia Prescott Turnbull, in _The Rector of Justin_ (chapter 12)[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Rector_of_Justin#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAuchincloss1964179-58)

Over the course of the novel, an increasingly immoral WASP establishment begins hiding behind moral individuals like Francis Prescott to obscure its own failures. Auchincloss wrote that the basic idea of the novel was "to study a saint and to leave it up to the reader whether saints are good or bad."[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Rector_of_Justin#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAuchincloss19689-59) By the end of the novel, Justinians have raised up an idealized version of Prescott to pretend that Christian values are still relevant to modern society, turning Prescott into "a symbol rather than a source of morality."[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Rector_of_Justin#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPiket1989190-60) Prescott's daughter Cordelia points out that the true elites have carefully sidelined her father, who was "not quite to be taken seriously".[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Rector_of_Justin#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAuchincloss1964179-58)

Removing Prescott from the picture clarifies that while the American elite's "inviolable rules of conduct ... were once the glue that held together a stern, but deeply felt system of ethical values," by the 1940s they were "little more than useful justifications for preserving a selfish status quo."[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Rector_of_Justin#cite_note-Kakutani-61) Auchincloss praised the writings of [Oliver La Farge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oliver_La_Farge "Oliver La Farge"), another unhappy Groton alumnus, which taught him that "Groton without Peabody" is "_just_ this 'dream', this stuffy little group of snooty, cruel boys".[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Rector_of_Justin#cite_note-:13-12)[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Rector_of_Justin#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGelderman199351-53-62)

Auchincloss' views evolved after the novel was published. After watching his high school classmates [William](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Bundy "William Bundy") and [McGeorge Bundy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McGeorge_Bundy "McGeorge Bundy") lead America into the [Vietnam War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vietnam_War "Vietnam War"), he concluded that the novel's take on Groton ("that its graduates were ... too shallow to aspire to the school's ideals") was fundamentally incorrect. He decided that "the ideals themselves were rotten",[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Rector_of_Justin#cite_note-:13-12) explaining that Groton taught the Bundys to never concede defeat, even when the war could not be won.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Rector_of_Justin#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAuchincloss201071-63) In _The House of the Prophet_ (1980), the novel's stand-in for [Walter Lippmann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Lippmann "Walter Lippmann") comments that the danger of Groton was in its culture of "pugnacity".[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Rector_of_Justin#cite_note-:13-12)

[![Image 6: Photo of Theodore Roosevelt, a supporter of Endicott Peabody](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/5b/Theodore_Roosevelt_by_the_Pach_Bros.jpg/250px-Theodore_Roosevelt_by_the_Pach_Bros.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Theodore_Roosevelt_by_the_Pach_Bros.jpg)

[Endicott Peabody](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endicott_Peabody_(educator) "Endicott Peabody (educator)")'s friend [Theodore Roosevelt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theodore_Roosevelt "Theodore Roosevelt") supported Peabody's goal to toughen up the children of American elites,[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Rector_of_Justin#cite_note-64) urging Peabody's students to avoid "the life of mere vapid ease."[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Rector_of_Justin#cite_note-65) However, some students questioned whether Peabody had been successful.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Rector_of_Justin#cite_note-:4-19)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Rector_of_Justin#cite_note-:5-20)

The novel reflects Auchincloss' disillusionment with American boarding schools' inability to live up to their founders' vision. In a 1968 essay,[[e]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Rector_of_Justin#cite_note-67) Auchincloss explained that "the central problem in all New England Protestant church schools of [Peabody's] day was the conflict between the piety and idealism of their inspirers and the crass materialism of the families" that supported them.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Rector_of_Justin#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAuchincloss19684-22) As [Gore Vidal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gore_Vidal "Gore Vidal") ([Exeter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phillips_Exeter_Academy "Phillips Exeter Academy") '43) put it, Auchincloss' books frequently trace "the collapse of the Puritan ethical system and its replacement by—as far as those of us now living can tell—nothing."[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Rector_of_Justin#cite_note-:22-68)

Like Prescott, the real-life Endicott Peabody sought to toughen up spoiled aristocrats through harsh discipline and simple living.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Rector_of_Justin#cite_note-:3-69)[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Rector_of_Justin#cite_note-70) Auchincloss suggested that this mission was doomed to fail, recalling Peabody "as a [David](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David "David") engaged in the seemingly hopeless struggle of preserving some degree of spirituality from the [Goliath](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goliath "Goliath") of materialism that re-invaded the school with each new form of prosperous youngsters."[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Rector_of_Justin#cite_note-:14-18) In the novel, Prescott contemptuously remarks that Peabody's Groton is "well equipped to train young men for the steam room of the Racquet Club".[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Rector_of_Justin#cite_note-:2-71) Only at the end of his life does Prescott realize that his school is no different.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Rector_of_Justin#cite_note-:1-34)[[f]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Rector_of_Justin#cite_note-73)

Auchincloss' upbringing was a case in point.
